cards.explanation: The answer is bad. Joseph, one of Jacob's sons, is seventeen and tending the flock with his brothers when he brings their father a bad report. The text says what kind of report it was but not what was in it. So I'm not going to make up the juicy details, friends, much as I'd love to. (Genesis 37:2)

The answer is a robe of many colors. Israel made Joseph a robe of many colors, and the text gives the reason: Joseph had been born to him in his old age. A rainbow robe? That's my kind of outfit, friends, though I'd get flour on it in about four seconds. (Genesis 37:3)

The answer is that they hate him. When Joseph's brothers see their father loves him more than any of them, they hate him. It's hard to read, friends, and it's what the text says. And it isn't the end of the feeling, because they'll hate him even more soon. (Genesis 37:4)

The answer is True. The text says Joseph's brothers “…could not speak a kind word to him.” Not a kind word, not even a small one. I think that must have made every day in the field feel long. (Genesis 37:4)

The answer is that they bow down to it. Joseph says, “…your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to mine.” His sheaf is standing tall while theirs gather around and bow. It's an unusual dream for a field of grain, friends. (Genesis 37:7)

The answer is True. The brothers ask, “Do you intend to reign over us?” and then, “Will you actually rule us?” Two questions back to back, and the text says they hated him even more because of his dream and his statements. I think they heard the dream loud and clear, friends. (Genesis 37:8)

The answer is stars. Joseph says the sun and moon and eleven stars were bowing down to him. That's his second dream, and it has a lot more sky in it than the first. I'll be honest with you, bakers, I'm partial to the stars. (Genesis 37:9)

The answer is False. After Joseph's second dream, his brothers did not warm up to him. The text says they were jealous of him. His father, on the other hand, kept in mind what Joseph had said. Jealousy on one side and a father turning it over on the other, friends. (Genesis 37:11)

The answer is to check on his brothers and the flocks. Israel says, “Go now and see how your brothers and the flocks are faring, and bring word back to me.” So Joseph's job is to look in and report. That's a simple errand with a long road ahead of it, friends. (Genesis 37:14)

The answer is Dothan. A man in the field tells Joseph, “They have moved on from here…” and says, “I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’…” So Joseph sets out after his brothers and finds them there. I'd say that stranger gave some really good directions, bakers. (Genesis 37:17)

The answer is that a vicious animal devoured him. The brothers say, “We can say that a vicious animal has devoured him.” It's a heavy plan, friends, so I'll just say that plainly. And keep that line in mind, because it comes back later in this story. (Genesis 37:20)

The answer is so he can rescue Joseph and return him home. First Reuben says, “Let us not take his life…” Then he suggests the pit, and the text says he said it “…so that he could rescue Joseph from their hands and return him to his father.” Reuben is Jacob's firstborn, so he's the oldest of the brothers. (Genesis 37:21-22; 35:23)
The answer is False. The text says, “Now the pit was empty, with no water in it.” So no water, just an empty pit. The text doesn't say more than that, friends, and neither will I. (Genesis 37:24)

The answer is Egypt. The caravan of Ishmaelites has camels carrying spices, balm and myrrh on their way down to Egypt. That means they're headed in a direction that's about to matter a lot, friends. (Genesis 37:25)

The answer is sell. Judah, another of Jacob's sons, says, “Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites and not lay a hand on him; for he is our brother, our own flesh.” And the brothers agreed. Judah's idea is to sell Joseph instead of killing him, and they go with it, friends. (Genesis 37:26-27)

The answer is twenty shekels of silver. The brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt. Twenty shekels, for a brother the text calls their own flesh. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the story, friends. (Genesis 37:27-28)

The answer is that he tears his clothes. When Reuben returns to the pit and sees that Joseph is not there, he tears his clothes. I think he's shaken to his bones. This is one of the heavy parts of the story, friends. (Genesis 37:29)

The answer is to dip it in the goat's blood. The brothers slaughtered a young goat and “…dipped the robe in its blood.” Then they sent the robe to their father and said, “We found this.” That's a hard moment, friends, and it's just what the text says. (Genesis 37:31-32)
The answer is True. Jacob recognizes the robe and says, “It is my son’s robe!” Then he says, “…a vicious animal has devoured him.” It's a painful verse to read, friends. (Genesis 37:33)

The answer is many days. The text says Jacob tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and “…mourned for his son many days.” His grief isn't a quick one. I think this is a verse to read slowly, friends. (Genesis 37:34)

The answer is False. His sons and daughters tried to comfort Jacob, but “…he refused to be comforted.” He says, “No… I will go down to Sheol mourning for my son.” Then the verse closes with “So his father wept for him.” It's a heavy moment, friends. (Genesis 37:35)

The answer is the guard. The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard. Joseph started the chapter tending flocks with his brothers, and now he's been sold in Egypt. That's a lot of road for one chapter, bakers. (Genesis 37:2, 36)
